newsitem.title: USA: Scientists prepare for Pathfinder landing on Mars.
newsitem.headline: Scientists prepare for Pathfinder landing on Mars.

text.p: Lights burned bright during the early hours of Friday morning at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena as scientists prepared for a unique exploration of the planet Mars.

With less than 24 hours before the probe slammed into the Red Planet, scientists were busy preparing for what they hoped would be a number of milestones in the exploration of Earth's closest planet. They include the first landing on a planet without orbiting it, the first time a remote controlled buggy has rumbled over the surface of an alien planet and the first time a parachute has been deployed at supersonic speeds, in this case at 1,000 miles per hour (2,896 kph).

The Pathfinder spacecraft, with its valuable cargo of the "Mars Buggy" and its host module, is due to hit Martian soil at 10:07 a.m. Pacific Daylight Time (1707 GMT) on Friday in a patriotic American Independence Day landing, just four minutes after slamming into the Red Planet's atmosphere at 16,000 mph (25,740 kph).

Scientists admit that America's latest venture to Mars -- the first in 21 years since a Viking mission landed there in 1976 and took blurry black and white pictures of Earth's nearest planetary neighbour -- is as full of hazards as Mars' crater-pockmarked surface.

"We don't really know where we are landing; we don't know what sort of terrain we are landing in, and we don't know what the atmosphere will be," explained Brian Muirhead, the Deputy Project Manager for the mission who is also in charge of managing how the flight goes, right down to the landing.
If Muirhead, his crew, and the Pathfinder perform as expected, and the conditions on the Red Planet are suitable, Pathfinder will touch down on the red dust of Mars in an area known as Ares Vallis.
If all goes according to plan, Pathfinder will deploy its parachute two minutes before landing and turn on its radar sensors 90 seconds later as it heads for the Martian surface.

Huge airbags surrounding the lander will be inflated just eight seconds before hitting the Martian surface. Pathfinder will initially bounce along the Martian surface like a beach ball, except that the bounces will start out at 40 feet (12 metres) high and 100 yards (90 metres) long.

But whether the landing has been successful will not be known for a nailbiting four-plus hours from the scheduled touchdown. Scientists explained that during the landing, the Earth will be on the Martian horizon and no communication with the spacecraft will be possible.

Whether the mission is a success or a failure, officials from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory as well as its parent body, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, say the Pathfinder mission to Mars will have established its goal. It will have established new technology for future space missions and proved that space can be explored without wasting taxpayer dollars.

The current Mars programme calls for 10 flights to the planet, both orbital and landing missions, over the next eight years. It is to culminate in a craft that will not only pick up Martian rocks but will return them to Earth, which will cost much less in current dollars than a single Apollo flight to the moon.
"We are back (on Mars), and we are back to stay this time," declared Wesley Huntress, the Associate Administrator for Space Science at NASA.

NASA Administrator Daniel Goldin, visiting the Jet Propulsion Laboratory for the landing, said failure of the Pathfinder mission was a possibility. However, if that happened it would have no effect on the long-term Mars exploration programme, he said.
"The success or failure of this first step doesn't relate to the total programme," Goldin said, adding that the programme was "tolerant" of a few failures.
"I want people to take risks. I want them to know that if they fail, we will come to them and shake their hands" he said.
